claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are caused by variations in short-range order.
Mechanical-property differences among these alloys are caused by variations in dislocation interactions.
The specific combination and concentration of alloying elements influence short-range order and dislocation interactions.
The compared quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are equiatomic, single-phase FCC materials after thermomechanical processing.
Removing one or more elements from equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni produces the proposed quaternary and ternary comparison alloys.
Short-range order and dislocation density are the structural mediators linking composition to mechanical behavior.
Dislocations glide and interact with short-range-order domains during deformation.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy will have greater tensile strength than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy will have greater ductility than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The magnitude of the mechanical-property differences depends on which elements are removed.
The proposed trends apply under room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing while the alloys remain single-phase FCC.
Processing history can influence short-range order and dislocation structure.
Secondary phases or impurities can affect the measured mechanical properties.
Failure of the alloys to follow the predicted strength and ductility rankings would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of correlation between short-range order or dislocation density and the predicted mechanical outcomes would falsify the hypothesis.
